text: When people talk about the printing press, they tend to imagine an overnight revolution, but the change was both deeper and slower than that picture suggests. What Gutenberg's movable type really did, starting around the 1450s, was collapse the cost of copying a text, so a book that once took a scribe months could now be produced in quantity. The first effect was simply more books, and then cheaper books, which over decades pulled reading out of the monasteries and into the hands of merchants, lawyers, and eventually ordinary literate townspeople.The speed is the part I find most interesting, because the technology spread fast even though its social consequences arrived slowly. Within about fifty years presses had reached most major European cities and had printed millions of volumes, yet the real shifts, like standardized spelling, a wider reading public, and the rapid circulation of Reformation pamphlets, unfolded across the following century. In other words, the machine was adopted in a generation, but the world it remade took several generations to settle into place.
